title: The training principles series: synergy
summary: NH defines synergy, an overarching principle above carryover and specificity: every lift in a program should be fed by others. Lifts standing alone are a waste, but too much synergy (too many variations or near-identical lifts) lowers frequency and raises overuse risk. Synergy remains subject to volume, intensity and frequency.

claims.claim: Synergy is an overarching principle; carryover and specificity sit beneath it as sub-products, letting you think about a program globally so every aspect works together.
Your body won't progress if your mind doesn't; most lifters stop at basic concepts and then wonder why they stall.
Every lift in a program needs other lifts feeding into it; a lift standing by itself is a bad choice and shouldn't be there.
Throwing in a movement pattern you never otherwise train to 'shock the muscle' means no progress on it, possible injury and wasted time.
Front rack holds are pointless if you don't front squat.

Pause squats done alone every 10 days may progress, but not optimally; paired with heavy regular squats they feed each other through similar patterns with different difficulty curves, loads and volumes.
Too much synergy is bad: with 15 squat variations you either do far too much volume or rotate so much that each lift is practiced about 3 times a year.
Synergy is not all-powerful; it is subject to volume, intensity and frequency, the levers that make or break a program, so always ask how tonnage is applied over time.
Deadlift and squat are synergistic because both train the lower body: a stronger squat carries to the deadlift up to a point, but nothing beats specificity.
The more similar two lifts are, the more synergy but the higher the overuse injury risk; a small joint-angle difference can keep tendons healthy while still building strength.
Synergy extends to details: similar foot stance on overhead press and squat, and grip widths on presses and pulls.
Outside lifting, parts of your life should also synergize, but anything good in too high a quantity becomes poison.
He is naming such concepts deliberately to build his own vocabulary for talking to viewers.
